texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Campa river between Anga and Magadha, and the naga world beneath
region.zh: 鴦伽與摩竭陀間之瞻波河及龍界

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A poor man, dazzled by the glory of the serpent king Campeyya, longs for that splendour and is reborn in the naga palace—then, loathing the reptile shape, keeps the fast-day vows on an ant-heap by the road, yielding his body to any who want it. A snake-charmer seizes and tortures him for a month's profit; his consort Sumana, warned by three signs, follows, and king Uggasena buys the serpent's freedom, visits the jewelled naga world, and asks why one so glorious would be a hermit.
summary.zh: 貧者慕詹波龍王榮耀，感生龍宮；旋厭蛇身，於路旁蟻垤持齋布薩，自捨其身任人取用。弄蛇婆羅門捕而虐之月餘以牟利；其妻須摩那依三兆知之，訴於空中；鄔伽 Sena 王以金贖之，並遊龍界，問其何捨殊榮而為苦行者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master praised certain lay Brethren who had taken the fast-day vows, telling how wise men of old renounced even a Serpent King's glory to keep them. Of old the river Campa ran betwixt Anga and Magadha, where the serpent king Campeyya reigned in a jewelled palace under the water. King Magadha, defeated in battle, rode his charger into the flooded stream, and the serpent king took him to his throne and comforted him: by the serpent's power Magadha slew his rival and ruled both realms, paying yearly tribute at a jewelled pavilion, while all beheld his glory. A poor man going down with the crowd coveted that splendour, and dying was reborn seven days later on the dead king's couch. Ashamed of the reptile shape his merit had won, he put it off and ruled the serpents; but the serpent maidens again broke his fast-day vows, till he resolved to keep them among men: on fast days he lay coiled on an ant-heap by the high road, saying, "Those who desire my skin or any part of me, let them take it; or if any would have me a dancing snake, let them make me so."

Villagers built a pavilion over him and worshipped him as a serpent king, and women craved sons by his aid. His consort Sumana, fearing the world of men, asked by what sign she should learn of danger, and he led her to a lucky pond: "If any one strike me, the water will become turbid. If a roc bird carry me off, the water will disappear. If a snake-charmer seize me, the water will turn to the colour of blood." Then a young brahmin of Benares, schooled at Taxila in the charm that commands all things of sense, caught him on his way home: the charm pierced his ears like burning splinters, yet the serpent shut his eyes and hooded his head lest his poison destroy the man and break his virtue. Spat upon and blained, squeezed with a goat's-foot staff, his teeth broken, dragged by a cord through his nostrils, he bore the torment and never glanced at his tormentor, lying month after month in a basket, dancing for money in village after village, refusing frogs that none might be killed for his sake, and food, that he might not die in the basket.

In a month the charmer came to Benares, and before the multitude at the palace court made the Great Being dance, while thousands waved kerchiefs and jewels showered about him. That day Sumana looked at the pond and saw the water red as blood; she traced his path, learned all in the frontier village, and came to Benares, where above the palace court in the air she stood lamenting. The serpent, ashamed, crept into his basket; the king, seeing the radiant shape in the sky, asked what she was. "No goddess I, nor Titaness, nor human, mighty king—a female of the serpent kind, come for a certain thing." He might burn the town to cinders, she said, but loves the holy way; caught on a holy day at the four-ways keeping his vows, he begs freedom. The king offered gold, a hundred kine, a village, jewelled earrings and thrones; the charmer wanted no gifts—the deed itself would be meritorious—and released the serpent, who shed his shape and stood a young man magnificently arrayed, swearing by wind-moving-mountains and sea-running-dry that he could never lie; and the king, believing, out of gratitude swore never to return ill for good.

Eager to visit the serpent's world, the king came with his army, and the Great Being made visible a wall of seven precious things, adorning all the approach; in Campeyya's halls, lit like the ruddy sun with a thousand perfumes and celestial harps, the king feasted seven days on divine food. On his fair seat he asked why one so glorious left such magnificence to lie on an ant-heap and keep the fast-day vows. "Not for life or sons or pelf do I wrestle with myself; 'tis my craving, if I can, to be born again as Man." "How does our world surpass thine?" "Comes control and cleansing when one is in the world of men, only there: once man, I'll never see nor birth nor death again." The king vowed henceforth to do manifold virtuous deeds; the Serpent King offered treasure without count—gold untold, pearls five thousand loads—to build houses of gold and enrich Benares, sending it loaded in hundreds of carts; from that time, they say, the ground was all golden throughout India. Devadatta was the snake-charmer, Rāhula's mother was Sumana, Sāriputta was Uggasena, and the Master was Campeyya, King of the Snakes.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the Ganges bank hermitage

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Four god-sons, promised to a childless chaplain by a bullied tree-deity, are named for elephant-, horse-, cow- and goat-herds and raised in those trades to keep them from the religious life. Yet Hatthipāla, offered the kingdom, refuses it—'death comes in youth as in age'—and renounces; one by one his brothers, the chaplain, the chaplain's wife, the king (taught by his queen's vulture parable), and the queen follow, until Benares stands empty and Sakka must build a hermitage thirty-six leagues long for the multitudes.
summary.zh: 樹神受迫而賜婆羅門四子，皆天神託生，取名養象、養馬、養牛、養羊，寄養各行以防出家。然長子 Hatthipāla 拒受王位，言「少年亦會死」，遂出家；諸弟、婆羅門夫婦、王（受王后禿鷹喻啟發）相繼棄俗，波羅奈城為之一空，帝釋遂為之營建三十六由旬精舍。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of the Renunciation, that it was not the first time he had made it. Of old, in Benares, king Esukārī and his chaplain, both childless and fast friends, bargained: if a son was born in the chaplain's house he should be lord of the kingdom, but if the king had a son he should be master of the chaplain's wealth. Meeting outside the south gate a wretched woman with seven hale sons begotten through prayer to the banyan tree, the chaplain for six days threatened to have the deity cut down and chopped piecemeal if no son was granted the king. The tree-goddess sought the Four Great Kings, the goblin war-lords, and at last Sakka, who found four meritorious god-sons—once weavers of Benares who had shared their winnings five ways—about to descend from the Heaven of the Thirty-three; they consented on their own terms: born in the chaplain's family, not the royal house, and renouncing the world while yet young. On the seventh day the goddess cleft the trunk and promised not one son but four, all to the chaplain, though they would never live in a worldly household.

The eldest, Hatthipāla, Elephant Driver, was entrusted to elephant-keepers to hinder his renouncing; Assapāla, the Groom, grew up among horse-keepers; Gopāla, the Cowherd, among cattle-breeders; Ajapāla, the Goatherd, among goat-herds. All ascetics were banished from the kingdom. When Hatthipāla was sixteen, king and chaplain, fearing royal splendour's confusions, disguised themselves as ascetics and went begging to his door; the lad welcomed them with delight, offering seats and water, till the chaplain revealed his purpose—to sprinkle him king if he saw him without renouncing. "Oh, my father, I want no royalty; I will renounce the world." "First learn the Vedas, get you wealth and wife and sons... sweet is the wood to live in then." "Truth comes not by the Vedas nor by gold; nor getting sons will keep from getting old; from sense there is release, as wise men know; in the next birth we reap as now we sow." And to the king's blessing—"may they see a hundred years of health in store for thee"—the prince answered that no man has a covenant with old age, and that as a ferryman's boat is left at the further shore, so mortals tend to sickness, old age and death.

So Hatthipāla departed to the Ganges bank with a league-long company, to wait for his brothers and all Benares. Then the test was repeated: Assapāla refused the umbrella his brother had spewed out—"pleasures of sense are but morass and mire"—and followed; Gopāla, like a man who has found his lost cow's track, said "never put off till the morrow what should be done to-day," and followed; Ajapāla, youngest, said death comes in youth as in age and none bears a mark of it, and followed. Then the chaplain, "a sonless man is a disbranched tree," led out sixty thousand brahmins; and the king, greedy for the chaplain's treasure, was taught by his queen a parable: she heaped dog's-flesh ringed with a snare, and the wise vultures, too heavy to rise, disgorged and flew free, while the fools that ate on were caught. "A brahmin vomits out his lusts, and wilt thou eat the same? He who eats a vomit, sire, deserves the deepest blame." Repenting, the king left his sovranty; the queen opened the storehouses and engraved on a golden plate where the treasure lay; and the whole city emptied itself, shops standing open, none turning to look.

The company grew till it covered thirty leagues; Sakka, perceiving what was afoot, ordered Vissakamma to build on the Ganges bank a hermitage six-and-thirty leagues long and fifteen broad, with leaf-huts, pallets, wells and fruit-trees, everything necessary for the religious, and to banish all hideous sounds and hateful beasts from the place. Hatthipāla entered by a footpath, took the ascetic's dress, and admitted the rest to the Brotherhood, setting apart huts for women with young boys, for old women, for the childless, and for the men. A certain king, hearing there was no king in Benares, came and was admitted with his band; six other kings joined them—these seven kings renounced their wealth—and Hatthipāla's teaching, quelling each arising thought of lust, saved the multitude from hell, from animal birth, from the ghost world and from Titan birth, two-thirds of them passing to the Brahma world. Of that time, king Suddhodana was Esukārī, Mahāmāyā his queen, Kassapa the chaplain, Sāriputta was Hatthipāla, Moggallāna was Gopāla, and the Master was Hatthipāla himself.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Lake Chaddanta in the Himalaya (legendary); Benares
region.zh: 雪山六牙池（傳說之地）與波羅奈

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The white six-tusked elephant king Chaddanta, slighted by his lesser queen Cullasubhaddā twice—with dry twigs instead of flowers, and a seven-shoot lotus given to her rival—vows rebirth as a queen of Benares and sends a hunter to kill him. The hunter Sonuttara journeys seven years, seven months and seven days, shoots him with a poisoned arrow from a pit, and the dying Bodhisatta, seeing the robber's yellow robe and feeling no anger, saws off his own six-rayed tusks as a gift toward Omniscience; the queen who receives them dies of grief that very day.
summary.zh: 白六牙象王遭次妃以枯枝代花、七莖蓮予妒妃之辱，誓生為波羅奈王后，遣獵人殺己。獵人跋涉七年七月七日，伏坑以毒箭射之；象王見其黃衣而不怒，忍痛自鋸六色光芒之象牙以施，發願趨一切智。后接牙當日心碎而亡。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A female novice of Sāvatthī, hearing the Law, suddenly recalled a former existence: in the time of Chaddanta the elephant she had been one of his wives, and she had harboured a slight grudge and sent a hunter who killed him with a poisoned arrow; she laughed, then wept aloud, and the Master, smiling, told the assembly, "This young Sister wept, on recalling a sin she once committed against me." Of old, by lake Chaddanta in the Himalaya, girt with seven mountains and ringed with leagues of lilies and lotuses, dwelt eight thousand royal elephants; their chief, the Bodhisatta, was pure white with red feet and face, eighty-eight cubits high, with a trunk like a silver rope and tusks thirty cubits long that emitted six-coloured rays; he honoured the pacceka buddhas and lived in a golden cave with his two head queens, Cullasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā.

Striking a sāl tree in full flower as the herd disported itself, the king showered flowers and pollen on Mahāsubhaddā, who stood to leeward, but on Cullasubhaddā, to windward, dry twigs, dead leaves and red ants; and when, after the bathing of the herd, an elephant offered him a seven-shoot lotus, he took it in his trunk, sprinkled the pollen on his forehead, and presented it to Mahāsubhaddā. Twice his lesser queen conceived a grudge. Entertaining five hundred pacceka buddhas, she put up a prayer over her gift of wild fruit: may I be reborn a royal maiden of the Madda line, become chief queen of the king of Benares, and send a hunter with a poisoned arrow to slay this elephant and have a pair of his six-rayed tusks brought me. She took no food, pined away, died, and was born as the Madda king's daughter Subhaddā, married to the king of Benares and chief of his sixteen thousand wives.

Recalling her former existences, she feigned sickness, and when the king promised all joys, she demanded that all the hunters of his three-hundred-league kingdom be assembled before she named her desire. Among the sixty thousand who came she spied Sonuttara, broad of foot, thick-bearded, scarred, once an enemy of the Great Being; from the topmost floor of the palace, hand stretched to the northern Himalayas, she described the seven mountains, the Golden Cliff, and the great banyan tree where the six-tusked white elephant dwelt with his herd of eight thousand, whose wrath would consume any man who saw them. Terrified, the hunter was reassured—her prayer to the pacceka buddhas would be fulfilled—and given a thousand pieces and a hogshead sack of provisions, leather ropes, elephant shoes and a parachute. Thrice sending back his retinues, he alone crossed eighteen wild regions, felled thickets, crossed morass and flood, and climbed mountain after mountain by grappling-iron, peg and rope, descending the last like a bird on his leather parachute.

After seven years, seven months and seven days the hunter dug a pit by the pool, and in false top-knot and yellow robes shot the king with a poisoned arrow. Mad with pain, the king had wellnigh slain him when a yellow robe met his eyes. Extinguishing his anger he asked why wounded: the queen of Kāsi, said the hunter, had dreamed of him and coveted his tusks. "Rich store of goodly tusks have I: 'tis at my life the wretch aims." He bade the hunter saw off his tusks before he died; the Great Being bent his body, let him climb his trunk, and guided the saw with his own trunk, cutting them off as it were sprouts. "I give them not because I value them not; the tusks of omniscience are a hundred thousand times dearer; may this deed win me Omniscience." By the tusks' magic the hunter reached Benares in seven days; his herd mourned him, and pacceka buddhas kept vigil at his pyre; and the queen, taking the six-rayed tusks on her fan, remembered her dear lord; her heart broke, and she died that day. The hunter is now Devadatta; the elephant was the Master.

title.en: Sambulā-Jātaka (The Devoted Wife and the Leper Prince)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: When leprosy drives the viceroy Sotthisena into the forest to die, his radiant wife Sambulā refuses to leave him and nurses him daily. An ogre seizes her at the bathing pool; her lament heats Sakka's throne, and the god drives the ogre off with his thunderbolt and chains him to a far mountain. Slandered as unfaithful, Sambulā performs an Act of Truth and heals the leprosy; back on the throne Sotthisena neglects her until his father rebukes him, and the pair live happily after.
summary.zh: 癩病襲儲君須提慎那，遁入林中待死；其妻三木羅不棄，日日侍疾。浴池畔為食人夜叉所執，其哀慟熱帝釋座，神以金剛杵逐之，鎖於第三重山。遭疑不貞，乃以真實語誓願癒其病。還宮後王疏遠之，老王出家為僧訓子，夫婦和樂終老。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of queen Mallikā, the devoted wife—"not now only, but formerly too, she was a devoted wife." Of old king Brahmadatta had a son named Sotthisena, made viceroy, whose chief consort Sambulā was so radiant she seemed a lamp-flame shining in a sheltered spot. Leprosy appeared, the physicians failed, and the loathsome prince cried, "What good is my kingdom to me? I shall perish without a friend in the wilderness," and left his harem. Sambulā, though he made many attempts to stop her, refused to return: "I will watch over you, my lord, in the forest," and went out from the city with him. In a leaf hut by a well-watered spot she rose early, swept the hermitage, ground simples and anointed his sores, gathered wild fruit, washed him with powders and clay, bathed his feet, and lay down by his side; thus she watched over her lord.

One day, bathing at a mountain cave, she lit the whole forest with the radiance of her person, and a goblin out hunting prey fell in love and questioned her from his hiding. She told him plainly: her lord lay sick in the forest, she tended him alone, and the venison in her basket was for him. "What good is this sick lord of thine to thee? No wife, but nurse is what he craves. I will thy husband be." She refused—he was worn and wretched, let the ogre woo some fairer dame—and when he threatened to eat her, seized her by the arm, she still deplored only that her dear lord's love should fall away. Then the abode of Sakka shook with the efficacy of her virtue, and the god came with all speed, thunderbolt in hand, and standing above the goblin threatened that his skull be riven into seven fragments if he touched her; the goblin let her go, and Sakka, thinking he would offend again, bound him with celestial chains and set him on the third mountain from thence.

Escaped from the ogre, she fled to her hut in the moonlight, lamenting like a bird that finds its fledglings dead, hailing priests and brahmins, tigers and grasses, Night and Ganges and Himavat in her sorrow. Sotthisena, suspecting a lover, put her to the test; she declared she was seized by the ogre and saved by Sakka, but he answered that womenkind are too clever and their truth a rarity. "Though you do not believe me, by virtue of the truth I speak, I will heal you." Filling a pot of water and performing an Act of Truth—"May Truth for aye my shelter be, as I love no man more than thee"—she poured the water on his head, and the leprosy left him as copper rust is washed away in acid. They returned to Benares; the king raised the umbrella over his son and made Sambulā chief queen by sprinkling, then himself adopted the ascetic life in the park.

But Sotthisena ignored her and took his pleasure with other women, and she grew thin and pale with jealousy till her veins stood out; to her father-in-law the ascetic she lamented that she no longer reigned in his affections. The old man rebuked his son: when you were crushed by leprosy and hid in the forest, she went with you and ministered to you, and by the power of truth healed your sickness, and now you do not even know the place of her sitting and uprising—an act of treachery to a friend like this is a sin. A loving wife is ever hard to find, he said; do thou, O king, to Sambulā be true. The king asked her pardon, conferred on her all power, and promised that he and the maidens would be obedient to her command; thenceforth the pair lived happily, and after a life of charity the ascetic passed to the heaven of Brahma. Sambulā of that time was queen Mallikā, Sotthisena the king of Kosala, and the ascetic father the Master.

title.en: Ummadantī-Jātaka (The Beauty and the King's Trial)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Aritthapura in the kingdom of the Sivis (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 濕毗國阿利陶城（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Ummadantī, of more than mortal beauty won by a half-robe given to a monk, is branded a witch by the dazed royal soothsayers and married to the commander Ahipāraka instead. At the Kattika festival she scatters flowers on the passing king, who loses his wits; Ahipāraka stages a hollow-tree oracle to spare him sin, and then, offering her as a free gift, refuses the king's relief until the king renounces the wrong—not for all the world would he do injustice—and so is cured of his infatuation.
summary.zh: 鬱摩達女因布施半衣與比丘而得絕世容貌；相士們見之失常，誣為妖婦，遂嫁統帥阿羅波羅迦。節慶之夜她向巡遊之王擲花，王遂神魂顛倒。統帥設空心樹神諭之計以護王免罪，並以妻相贈；王言「縱得全世，不行不義」，終斷痴念。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a backsliding Brother who, pierced with love's shafts for a woman seen on his alms round, wasted to a wild-deer leanness and gave up instruction and meditation. Of old, in Aritthapura in the kingdom of the Sivis, king Sivi made over his realm to his son, prince Sivi, who made his friend Ahipāraka commander-in-chief. In the same city dwelt the merchant Tiritavaccha, worth eighty crores, whose daughter Ummadantī was of more than mortal loveliness: all worldlings who beheld her were intoxicated as with strong drink. Sent for by the king to be tested by the fortune-tellers, she so unhinged the brahmins that some put their morsels on their heads and some threw them at the wall; furious, they told the king she was a witch, and she was not sent for—and she conceived a grudge, saying, "Should I ever see the king, I shall know what to do." Her father gave her to Ahipāraka, her husband's darling and delight.

Her beauty was the fruit of an old merit: once, a poor girl of Benares, laboring three years for a scarlet robe, met by the river a monk of Buddha Kassapa robbed of his garments and dressed in broken boughs; she tore her new robe in two and gave him half, then, seeing him blaze like the newly-risen sun, gave him the other half too, praying, "May I in some future existence be of such surpassing beauty that no one who sees me may have power to control himself, and no other woman be more beautiful." Born now in Aritthapura, at the Kattika festival her husband warned her not to show herself to the king; but when the king's chariot came first to their door in the moonlit procession, she stood at the window and threw flowers over him with all the charm of a sylph. The king, maddened with passion, failed even to recognise the house, asked his charioteer whose it was and whether the lady were unwed, and turning back from the festival lay on his couch chattering of Ummadantī: "I would be Ahipāraka one night or haply twain, and Ummadantī thus enjoyed, he might o'er Sivi reign."

Told that the king had gone only to his door, Ummadantī called him a pot-bellied fellow with huge teeth, and Ahipāraka saw that if the king did not get her he would die. "My duty is to restore him to life, if it can be done without sin on king or me." So he schooled a stout knave to sit within a hollow tree, a sacred shrine, and when the general made his offering and prayed to know why the king lay chattering, the knave delivered the lesson: your king is not sick but infatuated with your wife Ummadantī; if he gets her he will live, otherwise he will die. Repeating this as from the yakkha of the shrine, the servant secured the purpose, and Ahipāraka told the king the strange thing the yakkha had said. The king, shamed that his vileness was known to the very yakkhas, took his stand in righteousness—"Fallen from grace no godhead shall I win, and all the world will hear of my great sin"—and the two, in alternate stanzas, the general offering her as a free gift, the king pleading for his friend and his own honor, disputed the gift till dawn.

"Whoso shall wrong his neighbour nor repent, saying, 'See here a lord omnipotent,' will ne'er be found to live out half his days, and gods will view his conduct with dispraise," said the king. "I would not by an unjust act e'en heaven itself attain, no, not if, Ahipāraka, the whole world I should gain." Like the bull that leads the herd, so should the chief steer a direct course; father and chief and guardian of the land, he took his stand as champion of its rights, to his own will no more subservient: do righteously to parents, wife, children, friends, in war and travel, town and village, to brahmins and ascetics, to beasts and birds—thus heaven at last. When the king had thus been taught the law by his commander-in-chief, he got rid of his infatuation for Ummadantī. Of that time Ānanda was the charioteer Sunanda, Sāriputta was Ahipāraka, Uppalavaṇṇā was Ummadantī, and the Master was king Sivi.

title.en: Saṃkicca-Jātaka (The Sage and the Parricide King)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Prince Brahmadatta murders his father for the throne despite his friend Saṃkicca's warnings; haunted like Ajātasattu, he calls for the friend who fled to the Himalaya. Fifty years later Saṃkicca returns with five hundred ascetics, and to the king who asks how transgressors fare after death he preaches the eight great hells, the parricide's torments, the river Vetoaraṇī—and then, opening the earth, shows the angel-worlds—and the king is comforted.
summary.zh: 婆羅多太子不聽摯友僧祇叉之諫，弒父篡位；如阿闍世王般為怖所纏，遣人尋友。五十年後，僧祇叉率五百仙人歸，為王說八大熱獄、弒親之苦、地獄溫泉之河，復開地示天界；王心得安。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka containing vivid depictions of hell; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this in Jivaka's mango grove concerning Ajātasattu, who at Devadatta's instigation had murdered his own father, and after Devadatta was swallowed by the earth at the gate of Jetavana lived in terror, finding no enjoyment in his royal splendour, till he went by night to the Tathāgata and his fears abated. "Not now only, but of old too, this man, after murdering his father, through me recovered his peace of mind." Of old, in Benares, prince Brahmadatta and the priest's son Saṃkicca grew up together in the palace, great friends, schooled at Taxila; the prince was made viceroy and the Bodhisatta lived with him. One day, beholding his father's glory, the viceroy thought, "If I shall wait for his death, I shall be an old man before I succeed to the crown. I will kill my father and make myself king," and told his friend. "Friend, the murder of a father is a serious matter. That way lies the road to hell. You must not do this deed," said the Bodhisatta, opposing him a third time.

When the prince's attendants fell in with the plot and devised the murder of the king, the Bodhisatta thought, "I will not consort with people like these," and without taking leave of father or mother escaped by a house-door and hid himself in the Himalaya, where he embraced the ascetic life and attained the powers of ecstatic meditation, living on roots and wild berries; many youths of good family were ordained by him. The prince put his father to death and enjoyed great glory for a very short time; then he was terror-stricken, lost his peace of mind, and was like one who had found his punishment in hell. Calling to mind the friend who had tried to stop him, he sang his praises through harem and court and longed for him: if he had been here, he would not have let me slay my father, and he would free me from this terror.

After fifty years in the Himalayas the Bodhisatta thought, "The king remembers me. I must go to him and teach him the Law and remove his fears," and with five hundred ascetics passed through the air to the garden called Dayapassa. Warned by the garden-keeper, the king doffed the five emblems of royal pomp—umbrella, turban, yak-tail fan, shoes and sword—and came on foot to greet the sage, recalling the converse of old days. Then, as occasion arose, he put his question: "How fare transgressors after death? Born to what state are they? I too have erred from righteousness." "Mark, sire, and understand: shouldst thou point out the road to one gone hopelessly astray, and he should follow thy advice, no thorns beset his way... Right is like the high road, wrong is but a bye-road; right to heaven aye wins its way, wrong to hell leads men astray."

Then Saṃkicca told of the hells: Sañjīva, Kāḷasutta, Roruva, Saṅghāta, the Great Avīci, with Tapana and Patāpana—eight major hells, and sixteen times more the minor Ussadas—four-square with fourfold doors, walled and domed with iron no flame may melt, where all who have outraged saints fall headlong and rise no more, their mangled frames piecemeal like fish on toast; seeking outlet on every side, baffled at every door by barring gods. The parricide is boiled in an iron cauldron till he peels, pierced with steel shafts, blinded and fed on filth, a hot iron ball between his jaws while vultures rend his tongue; the matricide is ploughed with iron shares and given his own blood to drink; adulterers hang on the iron silk-cotton trees of the river Vetoaraṇī, and slayers of beasts are driven into a briny flood. "Through virtue stored on earth of old the good to heaven attain," and opening the earth he showed the king the angel-worlds: "bear righteous sway throughout thy realm, my king, for justice done is merit won, nor e'er regret will bring." The king was comforted, and the Master identified the Birth: Ajātasattu was the king, and the sage Saṃkicca was himself.

title.en: Kusa-Jātaka (The Ugly Prince and the Radiant Bride)

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Kusāvatī in the Malla country and Sāgala in Madda (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 末羅國拘舍婆提城與摩達國娑伽羅城（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Granted by Sakka a wise but ugly son, king Okkāka's queen seeks a bride as lovely as the golden image her son himself has wrought—and finds Pabhāvatī, whose radiance lights a dark room. Hid from her by day, Kusa is discovered at a lotus-pool; she flees home, and he follows as a humble cook in her father's palace for seven months, until Sakka's ruse brings seven suitors with armies and her father threatens to hack her in seven pieces—whereupon she reveals the 'slave' as the lion-voiced king, who routs them all and marries off her seven sisters to the seven kings.
summary.zh: 天帝賜與智慧而貌醜之子菅草；其自鑄金像遍尋天下，終得容光可照暗室之婆薮跋提。因其例禁晝見，象糞馬糞戲之、騎象窺之、蓮池擒之，她終遁回母國。菅草化名入宮為庖丁七月；帝釋計使七王來求婚，父怒欲分尸七段遣之，她乃揭穿「賤役」實為獅吼之王。王大破七軍，以其七妹配七王，夫婦和樂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka linked by commentators to Beauty-and-the-Beast tale-types; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a backsliding Brother smitten by a fair lady: through love of a woman, mighty sages of old lost their power and came to misery. Of old, in the Malla kingdom, king Okkāka's realm lacked an heir; dancing women were exposed in vain, and queen-consort Sīlavatī herself was exposed with religious sanction. Her virtue heated Sakka's throne; the god, disguised as an aged brahmin, took her hand before the jeering crowd, caused a hut to appear, and carried her to the heaven of the Thirty-three, where on the seventh day she knew him and asked a son. "Not merely one, lady: one wise but ugly, the other handsome but a fool; which first?" "The wise one." Sakka gave her kusa grass, a heavenly robe, sandal-wood, a coral-tree flower and a Kokanada lute, and bore her back to the king's couch; in ten months she bore a son named for the grass, Kusa, and later a second, Jayampati. Kusa, so wise that untaught he mastered every art, at sixteen was to receive the kingdom—but he had fashioned of gold a female image of matchless beauty, and vowed to wed only a woman like it.

The councillors bore the image through India; everywhere the people admired the divine nymph, but nowhere could they match her to any daughter—till at Sāgala in Madda the humpbacked nurse, sent for water, struck the golden image, her runaway foster-child, on the cheek; finding it gold, she boasted her Pabhāvatī, eldest of the Madda king's seven daughters, worth a sixteenth part more. The envoys rejoiced, the marriage was contracted, and queen Sīlavatī made a family observance the condition: no wife might see her husband by daylight till she had conceived. So Kusa reigned with Pabhāvatī, meeting her only in the dark, lest his bride see his radiance. Yet he longed to see her, and his mother's devices told against her: in the elephant-stall he pelted her with dung, in the stable with dirt; when his handsome brother rode by she saw only the impertinent elephant-keeper—Kusa himself, betraying his joy with gesticulating hands; in the lotus-pool, hidden by a leaf, he seized her hand: "I am king Kusa." She cried, "A goblin is catching hold of me," swooned, and fled home to her father that day; and Kusa, too proud to hold her, let her go, vowing to win her back.

Her scorn had old roots: in a former birth, when his sister-in-law gave his cake to a paccekabuddha, he snatched it back in anger—hence his ugliness—and prayed that wherever she dwelt he might carry her off as bride. In sorrow he took a thousand pieces, his five weapons and his Kokanada lute, traveled a hundred leagues a day, and entered Sāgala as minstrel, then apprentice potter, basket-maker and gardener, each time making work for her hand, which she threw down in rage while her sisters laughed. As the king's cook he surpassed himself, and climbing to the princesses' dwellings was reviled by Pabhāvatī: "Kusa, for thee by day and night to bear this burden is not right; haste back to Kusāvatī; thy ugly form I loth to see." "Bound by thy beauty's spell, Pabhāvatī, my native land has little charm; Madda's fair realm is ever my delight, my crown resigned, to live in thy dear sight," he answered. The humpbacked slave, bribed with a golden necklace, praised him through thirteen stanzas—"Esteem him not by outward form or height, Pabhāvatī; great glory his, so do whate'er is pleasing in his sight"—till her mistress cowed her with threats of a cut tongue.

After seven months of servitude Sakka intervened, sending seven kings, each privately, word that Pabhāvatī had cast off king Kusa and was to be wed. All seven arrived, discovered the trick, and invested the city; Madda's ministers counseled surrender, but the king swore to slay her and send a piece of her to each suitor, and the executioner was summoned. Her mother, lamenting her beauty doomed to the vultures, cried, "Where's he that crushes hostile realms? Kusa the wise would free us from our woes." "The conqueror who crushes all his foes—lo, here is he," said Pabhāvatī, pointing through the window at the pot-bellied cook; her father humbled himself before the disguised king, and Pabhāvatī groveled in the mud at Kusa's feet and begged pardon. Kusa, lion-like, mounted a war-elephant with Pabhāvatī behind, and roared thrice: warriors, horse and foot broke and fled, and Sakka, glad, gave him the gem Verocana. He took the kings alive, and bestowed Pabhāvatī's seven sisters on them; riding home in one car, neither outshone the other, both alike fair, and in peace and plenty they lived happily. The humpback of that tale was Khujjuttarā, Pabhāvatī was Rāhula's mother, and king Kusa was the Master.

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: River Rohinī between Kapilavatthu and Koliya; the Himalaya Red Valley
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛與拘利之羅希尼河；雪山紅谷

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A quarrel over the Rohinī dam brings the Sākya and Koliya hosts to battle, until the Buddha, seated cross-legged in the air between the armies, quells the feud with five birth-stories and the Attadaṇḍa Sutta; five hundred young Sākyans he ordains, but their hearts still cling to their wives, so he carries them to the Himalaya and has the bird-king Kuṇāla—escorted through the sky by three thousand five hundred hen-birds—preach at vast length the faithlessness of women, from the lady with five husbands who sinned with a humpbacked slave to the nun Saccatāpavī, curing the monks of their discontent.
summary.zh: 羅希尼河堤之爭幾釀釋迦與拘利兩族之戰；佛陀於兩軍之間凌空結跏，以五本生及不害偈平息爭端，度五百釋子出家。然彼等猶念舊妻，佛乃攜之至雪山，由眾鳥護送之孔雀王說婦人薄倖，自五夫之婦至白衣尼諸例，僧眾之不樂遂息。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka containing a lengthy polemic against women characteristic of its monastic milieu; presented here as historical scripture of a living tradition and not endorsed as present-day teaching; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Sākya and Koliya tribes watered their crops by a single dam on the river Rohinī, and in Jetthamūla, as the crops drooped, the labourers quarrelled over the water—taunts flying about the origin of each royal house—till the councillors told the princes, and both tribes sallied forth. At dawn the Buddha, watching the world from Sāvatthī, saw them setting out and resolved to quell the feud; he went alone and sat cross-legged in the air between the hosts, shrouding the sky with rays from his hair, then revealing himself in six-coloured radiance. Both armies threw down their arms—"the Master, our noble kinsman, is come: let the others slay us or roast us alive"—and seated on a sand-bed throne he asked: what was the quarrel? About the water. What is the water worth? Very little. The earth? Priceless. Warrior chiefs? Priceless. "Why for some worthless water would you destroy chiefs of high worth?" He told them three birth-stories to appease the quarrel and two on the blessings of unity, finished with the Attadaṇḍa Sutta, and each people offered him two hundred and fifty youths, whom he ordained—five hundred Brethren who took orders more from respect for the Teacher than pleasure.

Their former wives sent messages that stirred their discontent. "I will lead these Brethren to the Himalayas and illustrate the sins of womankind by the Kuṇāla story," resolved the Master, and carried them through the air over Himalaya's mountains, rivers and lakes, till the longing for their wives passed off at that sight. In the Red Valley, under a sāl tree lasting an aeon, he had them ask of some marvel; two spotted cuckoos flew past bearing their lord on a stick between them. "This is an ancient custom of our family; in a former age three thousand five hundred hen-birds escorted me." Of old in that Himalaya lived the bird Kuṇāla, bright and gay-feathered, with three thousand five hundred hen-birds in attendance: two bore him on a stick, five hundred below to catch him if he fell, five hundred above against heat, as many on either side against wind and dust, five hundred before against stones, five hundred behind with cheering words, and five hundred more flying to and fro with fruits of every kind—yet day by day he upbraided them: "Perish, ye vile creatures... ungrateful for kindness done, going like the wind whithersoever ye list."

His friend, the royal cuckoo Punnamukha, reproached him for speaking ill of well-conducted ladies, and was abused in turn as won over by women's prayers. Soon Punnamukha fell sick unto death with a bloody flux—and his attendants left him alone and went over to Kuṇāla, whom he cursed for fickleness; then Kuṇāla drew near, took him up with wings and beak, and gave him medicines of every kind till his sickness was relieved. Restored, Punnamukha disowned the rogues who had left him, and Kuṇāla said, "Well then, friend, I will tell you of the wickedness of womenfolk," and brought him to the Red Valley, where a heavenly proclamation ran through the Himalayas that Kuṇāla, king of birds, seated on a rock of red arsenic, would preach the Law with a Buddha's charm. The gods of the six worlds assembled, and the vulture-king Ānanda with ten thousand vultures, and the ascetic Nārada with a thousand; and the Great Being, making Punnamukha his witness, related from his own remembrance of former births: "I have seen Kaṇhā, her that had a double parentage and five husbands, and whose affection was set upon a sixth man, a headless crippled dwarf."

The sermon unfolded story after story: Kaṇhā, daughter of a captive queen, threw her wreath on Pandu's five sons and wedded all five—yet, fired with lust for the humpback, promised each in secret the kingdom, and gave the humpback a sign with her tongue which Ajjuna alone divined; the five, learning this, renounced the world for the Himalayas. The white-robed nun Saccatāpavī was won in six days by a disguised goldsmith who swore false fasts and years; led drinking through the city, she lost a wise man his thousand-crown wager. Kurangavī, king's daughter, loved the low-born Elakamara, and sinned with his teacher and his attendant. And Pāticapā, wife of two kings by arbitration, sinned in mid-passage with the lame bald pilot. "With what vile wretch would she not misbehave?" sang the bird-king, who in those tales had been goldsmith, garuḍa, Ajjuna and Baka. The vulture-king Ānanda took up the theme—"Trust not a woman though she has borne ten children to thee... they court the man they hate as much as one they adore, even as a ship that hugs alike the near and farther shore"—and the five hundred Brethren's discontent was cured. The Master was the bird Kuṇāla.
